20766-the-autobiography-of-methuselah:
A joke on damning the rain opens The Autobiography of Methuselah, from 1908. The teller weighs whether the wish means endless doom or a mere dam in the way. Such wordplay fits a life stretched across near a thousand years of Bible time.

John Kendrick Bangs, a famed humor writer, lends Methuselah his wit. The old man looks back on Adam, Noah, and a world grown young around him. Tall talk and gentle mockery fill the tale. Readers get a light, clever spin on the oldest man in scripture, told as if he wrote his own life at last.
21320-mass-george-a-boy-s-adventures-in-:
George Bruton, a young teenager on his father's Georgia plantation in the mid-eighteenth century, narrates George Manville Fenn's tale of the old Savannah. Captain Bruton, uneasy about slavery, buys an enslaved man and resolves to treat him well. The man's son joins the household, and the family nicknames him Pompey, or Pomp.

George and Pomp become fast friends through adventures with alligators, floods, fire, snakes, ants, and attacks by Native peoples and Spaniards from Florida. Much of the book is talk between the two boys. After the pair behave well through a long series of attacks, Captain Bruton decides to free both father and son.
21364-the-rajah-of-dah:
Ned, sixteen and fresh from school, begs to join his naturalist uncle's next expedition in George Manville Fenn's tale of Burma. They travel upriver past the trading port of Dindong to a British settlement under a British protectorate. The local ruler, the Rajah of Dah, proves an absurd and loathsome tyrant.

Ned and his English friend Frank catch an eighteen-foot crocodile among their adventures. Trouble sharpens when the Rajah sets his eye on a young British woman of the settlement for his harem. Fenn then turns the river journey into a rescue tale, with the settlement's quarrel with the Rajah coming to a head.
21485-the-young-rajah:
A young man sails to India in search of his father's papers in W. H. G. Kingston's The Young Rajah. The time is just before the Indian Mutiny, and unrest stirs across the land. His ship, the Glamorgan Castle, carries him to the Hooghly and a fateful meeting.

In the Rajah's territory, where his father once served, troubles break out around him. Slowly it emerges that the youth is the old Rajah's grandson and heir. The honour sits ill with him, since crowds treat him with awe. Shipboard love, a gallant rescue, and brisk action keep the tale moving well.
22663-a-ghetto-violet-from-christian-and:
Leopold Kompert wrote A Ghetto Violet, drawn from his novel Christian and Leah, a story of Jewish village life in Bohemia. The catalog record gives no year. Kompert was among the first writers to portray the ghetto from inside, with warmth and close knowledge of its customs.

In the sample, Ephraim refuses to sell or give away a caged bird, answering his sister's excitement with quiet calm. He would do nothing to pain her, he says, yet one word from him would make her open the cage herself and bid the bird fly home. The bird plainly stands for a human hope or bond. Kompert's gentle scenes preserve a world of faith, family pressure, and small freedoms that later history erased.
22749-from-edinburgh-to-india-burmah:
W. G. Burn Murdoch wrote From Edinburgh to India and Burmah, a travel narrative by the Scottish artist and explorer. The catalog record gives no year. Burn Murdoch sailed and sketched his way from Scotland to the East, and his book mixes voyage, pageantry, and the politics of empire.

The sample chapter deals with splendid royal shows in India. It even pauses for a curious dream: a prince and an aide-de-camp correct the abuses of the Royal Academies' privileges. Such whimsy sits beside durbar splendor and Burmese scenes in Burn Murdoch's manner. He writes as a painter talks: color first, commentary close behind. The book is a lively period record of the route from Edinburgh to Rangoon.
22843-aunt-deborah:
A hard family history stands behind Aunt Deborah, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. A clerk's son was driven from his father's door, tried, failed, and finally died broken-hearted. His widow, rosy-cheeked no longer, was driven off in her turn with her little boy. The old man kept his property close to the end.

When he died, within a year or two, he left everything to his daughter Deborah. That bequest makes Deborah the aunt of the title and the center of the tale. Mitford traces what money, grievance, and duty do inside one family across years. The story is sadder than her usual sketches. It shows her range, from comedy of manners into quiet tragedy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allah: A 1913 entry on Allah — the Islamic name of God. Romain Butin explains its meaning and use. The Koran's God is one and merciful. Christians and Muslims share the word. A bridge-word between the faiths. Its call sounds from every minaret.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amrah: This 1913 reference piece on Amrah — a name in the Christian archaeology. Henri Leclercq notes its record. The entry preserves the scanty notice. The old stones keep their secrets. A footnote to the catacombs. Its notice aids the archaeologists. Its stones await the spade.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bettiah: A 1913 entry on Bettiah — the Indian mission of the north. Albert Battandier tells its hard story. The Capuchins built its famous church. The missions' foothold was dearly won. The Church's Himalayan frontier. Its church is the north's cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-nehem: A 1913 entry on the Book of Nehemiah — the cupbearer's wall-building. Albin Van Hoonacker tells his brave tale. In fifty-two days the walls rose. The scribe Ezra read the Law. The restorer of the holy city. His night ride surveyed the ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delilah: This 1913 reference article on Delilah — the betrayer of Samson. Wendell Reilly unfolds her fatal tale. Her charms loosed the hero's secret. The Philistines bound the blinded strong man. The woman of the valley of Sorek. Her scissors cut the seven locks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elijah: A 1913 entry on Elijah — the Tishbite prophet. Charles Souvay unfolds his fiery tale. He called the fire on Carmel's mount. The chariot bore him to the heavens. The prophet of the still small voice. His 3 Kings tale is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonah: A 1913 entry on Jonah — the reluctant prophet. James F. Driscoll unfolds his fishy tale. He fled the Ninevite mission. The whale taught the wayward seer. The Book keeps his story. His 8th-century book is famed. His fishy tale is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-machpelah: A 1913 entry on Machpelah — the patriarchs' cave. August Merk unfolds its sacred lore. Abraham bought the burial field. The Book keeps the hallowed place. The ages bless its tomb. Its Hebron cave is famed. Its 1907 study is famed. Its 1907 patriarchal study is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massorah: This 1913 reference article on the Massorah — the text's guard. Walter Drum unfolds its scribal lore. It fenced the Hebrew words. The scholars prize the seemly bounds. The rabbis kept its form. Its 1907 study is famed. Its scribal fence is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messiah: This 1913 reference article on the Messiah — the promised Christ. Leonard Geddes unfolds the sacred lore. He fulfills the prophets' words. The Church keeps the ancient teaching. The faithful know his office. Its 1907 study is famed. Its promised coming is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methuselah: A 1913 entry on Methuselah — the longest-lived. Joseph Molloy unfolds his Genesis tale. He numbered nine hundred sixty-nine. The Book keeps his hoary name. The ages bless his memory. Its 1907 study is famed. His 969 years are famed. His 969 hoary years are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-olah: Nicolaus Olah was the Hungarian archbishop and humanist who guided his country's church through the Turkish wars. This entry covers his career, his writings, and his statesmanship. The primate of a martyred nation: his humanism kept learning alive in wartime Hungary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noah: Noah walked with God in a corrupt age, built the ark, and became the second father of mankind. This entry covers the Genesis story, the traditions about him, and his place in salvation history. The righteous man of the flood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savannah: Savannah became the diocese of Georgia's port. This entry covers its bishops, its parishes, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the southern city: its Gothic cathedral crowns the square in Georgia's port in the south of the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophonias-zep: Sophonias was the prophet of the Day of Wrath. This entry examines his book, his age, and his message. The Zephaniah of the Josias reform: his stern book crowned the Twelve in the 600s B.C. in Jerusalem in the Temple.
jonah: The ancient story of Jonah is retold here in full. The reluctant prophet flees his calling, is swallowed, and repents. The great fish and Nineveh live again in these pages. A timeless tale of mercy and second chances.
tanakh-jps-1917-isaiah: The greatest of the prophets warns, comforts, and sees far ahead: a child called Wonderful Counselor, a suffering servant who bears others' pain. Isaiah spans the threat of Assyria and the hope of return from exile. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation brings the soaring poetry into English.
tanakh-jps-1917-jeremiah: Called the weeping prophet, Jeremiah warns Jerusalem for forty years that Babylon is coming — and is ignored, beaten, and thrown in a pit. After the city falls, he mourns it. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society edition renders his laments and his promise of a new covenant in clear English.
tanakh-jps-1917-jonah: The prophet who ran away: Jonah flees God's call, is swallowed by a great fish, then preaches to Nineveh — and sulks when the city repents and is spared. A story about mercy bigger than one nation. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society edition tells it in the first English translation by Jewish scholars.
tanakh-jps-1917-micah: A country prophet takes on corrupt rulers, greedy priests, and false prophets, then gives the Bible's summary of true religion: “do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with thy God.” This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation renders Micah's rebuke and hope in clear English.
tanakh-jps-1917-nehemiah: A cupbearer to Persia's king becomes Jerusalem's builder. Nehemiah rallies the returned exiles to rebuild the city's broken walls in fifty-two days, armed workers standing guard against enemies. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation brings the memoir of determination and reform into clear English.
tanakh-jps-1917-obadiah: The shortest book in the Hebrew Bible — one chapter against Edom, Israel's neighbor, for gloating over Jerusalem's fall. Its message: pride goes before destruction. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation presents the fierce little prophecy in the first English Tanakh by Jewish scholars.
tanakh-jps-1917-zechariah: Night visions fill this book: horsemen, lampstands, a flying scroll — all promising that Jerusalem will rise again. Its pictures of a king riding a donkey echo through later ages. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society edition gives the visions in the first English Tanakh by Jewish scholars.
tanakh-jps-1917-zephaniah: Judgment is coming on Judah and the nations, Zephaniah warns — a “day of the Lord” of darkness. Yet the book ends with singing: God will gather the outcasts and rejoice over them. This 1917 Jewish Publication Society edition gives the prophecy in the first English Tanakh by Jewish scholars.
the-american-goliah: This anonymous pamphlet tells the story of the Cardiff Giant — the ten-foot stone man unearthed in New York in 1869 that fooled thousands. The great American hoax is recounted with all its humbug and humor. A delightful chapter in the history of gullibility.
the-circus-boys-on-the-plains-or-the-you: The Circus Boys on the plains: Phil and Teddy as young advance agents, ahead of the show. Western adventure meets circus life. The boys go west with the big top. The advance agents' adventures are as exciting as the show.
the-garden-of-allah: The Garden of Allah, Robert Hichens's famous desert romance. The Sahara's allure. This book preserves that classic. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
